result: The Box C/D RNP assembled with st-sR26 transitions from a di-RNP to a mono-RNP upon substrate RNA binding, as demonstrated by SAXS and SANS measurements showing Rg reductions from 54.3 Å (apo) to 47.3-50.0 Å (half-loaded) and 45.0 Å (holo). The guide sequence strongly influences the oligomerization state of the holo complex.
evaluation: Claims C31-C42 provide converging evidence from SAXS (C31-C34), SANS P(r) distributions (C42), and comparison to theoretical Rg distributions (C35) that consistently demonstrate the di-RNP to mono-RNP transition. The guide sequence dependence is supported by experiments with st-sR26-1 and st-sR26-2 variants (C38-C41). The quantitative Rg values and their interpretation are well-supported by the data.

result: The st-sR26 RNP methylates substrate D' more efficiently than substrate D, with methylation levels depending on the nature of the first base-paired nucleotide of the substrate. Substrate D' with 5'-uridine displays good turnover in all conditions, while substrate D with 5'-guanosine requires binding of substrate D' for turnover.
evaluation: Claims C43, C100, C101, C113 are supported by citations to prior work (Graziadei et al., 2016) demonstrating differential methylation efficiency. Claims C102-C104 regarding turnover differences are also cited from the same prior work. These establish the functional context for the structural studies but rely on previously published data rather than new experiments in this manuscript.

result: The interaction interfaces of Nop5-CTD with L7Ae-K-turn-RNA and Nop5-NTD with fibrillarin are conserved relative to crystal structures, as validated by NMR chemical shift perturbations. A total of 407 and 442 PREs were collected for the D-loaded and D'-loaded mono-RNPs, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C44-C48 are supported by NMR CSP data (Figures 2—figure supplements 1 and 2) that map to known interaction interfaces from crystal structures. The assumption of conserved interfaces is validated experimentally. Claims C49-C50 provide quantitative data collection metrics. The evidence is internally consistent and well-documented.

result: NMR spectroscopy reveals that fibrillarin recognizes the substrate-guide duplex, with moderate chemical shift perturbations localized to residues V110, V151, and V185. PRE data indicate the presence of conformers in which fibrillarin is bound to the substrate-guide duplex.
evaluation: Claims C51-C57 are supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2a and PRE data in Figure 2b. The CSPs are consistent with expected proximity of specific methyl groups to RNA (C53-C54), and the PRE intensity ratios provide evidence for fibrillarin binding (C57). The inference that fibrillarin recognizes the substrate-guide duplex (C56) is well-supported by the pattern of CSPs.

result: Structure calculations yielded [on,off]-state ensembles defined to better than 2.5 Å RMSD precision, compatible with 400/407 (substrate D) and 436/442 (substrate D') PRE restraints. The structures show reasonable similarity to the S. solfataricus holo mono-RNP (PDB 3pla) but differ in many details, demonstrating sRNP architectural flexibility.
evaluation: Claims C58-C62 provide quantitative metrics for structure quality and restraint satisfaction. Claims C63-C66 compare the solution structures to the crystallographic structure, noting both conservation of major features (C64) and differences in details (C65). The inference of architectural flexibility (C66) is supported by the observed structural differences. The precision and validation metrics are appropriate.

result: Neither [on,off]- nor [off,off]-ensembles alone can reproduce the combination of PRE and SAS data satisfactorily. While [on,off]-structures fit PRE data reasonably well, they fail to fit 2H-Fib SANS and SAXS curves, indicating the presence of conformational ensembles related to fibrillarin position.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 demonstrate that single conformational states are insufficient to explain the data. The evidence from Figures 3—figure supplements 3-5 shows good PRE fits (C68) but poor SAS fits (C69) for [on,off]-structures. The inference that conformational ensembles are required (C70) and that they relate to fibrillarin position (C71) is logically supported by the pattern of data agreement/disagreement.

result: Ensemble scoring for the substrate D'-loaded sRNP yielded best-fit ensembles containing 66 ± 8% [on,off]-conformers, showing much improved fit to SAXS and 2H-Fib SANS curves and improved PRE agreement. An acceptable fit requires the combination of both [on,off]- and [off,off]-conformers.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by data in Figures 4 and 5 showing improved fits to both SAS and PRE data. Claim C75 is supported by control experiments (C76) demonstrating that ensembles containing only one conformer type fail to fit the data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The quantitative population estimate (66 ± 8%) is derived from the ensemble scoring algorithm.

result: The substrate D-loaded sRNP shows a lower proportion of fibrillarin bound to the substrate-guide duplex (34 ± 10% [on,off]-conformers) compared to the substrate D'-loaded sRNP (66 ± 8% [on,off]-conformers). Fibrillarin binds more strongly to the substrate D'-guide duplex than to the substrate D-guide duplex in the context of the Box C/D RNP.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 are supported by PRE data showing higher intensity ratios for substrate D (C77), ensemble scoring results (C80-C81, Figures 4-5), and control experiments (C78-C79). The conclusion that fibrillarin binds more strongly to substrate D' (C82) is well-supported by the quantitative difference in [on,off]-state populations. The error estimates (±8-10%) provide appropriate uncertainty quantification.

result: MD simulations reveal that in the [off,off]-state, the substrate-guide duplex forms a regular A-form helix, but fibrillarin binding pushes the duplex toward the Nop5 coiled-coil, perturbing base-pairing at the substrate 3' end. The substrate D'-loaded complex shows disruption of two base-pairs at the 3' end and formation of many protein-RNA contacts, while the substrate D-loaded complex shows less extensive melting and fewer contacts.
evaluation: Claims C83-C92 are supported by MD simulation data shown in Figures 6 and 7. The differential behavior of substrate D' versus D is clearly documented, with substrate D' showing more extensive base-pair disruption (C86, C89) and more protein-RNA contacts (C87, C90). The observations are consistent with the experimental finding of differential fibrillarin binding affinity. The 150-ns simulation length is reasonable for observing these structural changes.

result: The stability of the fibrillarin-bound form depends on a delicate balance between entropy loss, base-pair melting, and formation of new protein-RNA contacts. The free energy difference for the [off,off]→[on,off] transition between substrate D'- and D-loaded complexes is only 0.86 ± 0.55 kcal/mol, suggesting that fine differences in substrate-guide helix stability may regulate fibrillarin affinity and the fractional population of active enzyme.
evaluation: Claim C94 is a reasonable inference from the MD simulations and structural analysis. Claim C95 is calculated from the population ratios using standard thermodynamic equations, with appropriate error propagation. The small ΔΔG value supports the speculation (C96) that fine differences in helix stability could regulate enzyme activity. However, C96 is speculative and would benefit from additional experimental validation of the proposed regulatory mechanism.

result: The affinity of fibrillarin for the substrate-guide helix depends on the RNA sequence outside the methylation site in the context of the Box C/D RNP, and the extent of fibrillarin binding correlates with methylation efficiency. This difference in affinity is explained by the energetics of a global conformational transition from an inactive to an active state.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C106-C109 represent the primary conclusions of the study. They are supported by the ensemble structures showing differential fibrillarin binding (C81-C82), MD simulations revealing sequence-dependent stability differences (C86-C92), and thermodynamic analysis (C95). The correlation between fibrillarin binding extent and methylation efficiency (C107) is supported by prior work (C43, C113). The mechanistic explanation (C109) is a well-supported inference from the structural and thermodynamic data.

result: An iterative structure-calculation protocol and ensemble structure-calculation method were developed that exploit integrative structural biology to characterize conformational ensembles. The combination of NMR PRE and SAS data was essential for revealing the equilibrium between RNA-bound and RNA-unbound fibrillarin states. The methodology is anticipated to be generally applicable to modular enzymes undergoing domain reorientation.
evaluation: Claims C8, C110, C128 describe the methodological development, which is documented in the Methods section and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. Claim C129 is supported by the demonstration that neither PRE nor SAS data alone could define the conformational ensemble. Claim C130 accurately describes the capability of the method. Claim C131 is speculative about broader applicability but is a reasonable extrapolation. The methodology represents a significant technical advance.

result: The copy of fibrillarin at the substrate-loaded site exchanges between substrate-bound and unbound states, with the substrate D'-loaded complex displaying a higher population of the methylation-competent [on,off]-state. The proportion of methylation-competent complex is subtly tuned by the free-energy difference between active and inactive conformations. Fibrillarin binding is accompanied by entropy loss and deviation from ideal A-form geometry, with base-pairs beyond the tenth being melted.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 summarize the major findings supported by the ensemble analysis (C72, C80-C81). Claim C114 correctly notes that crystallography cannot detect such dynamic equilibria. Claims C115-C119 provide mechanistic insights supported by the structural analysis and MD simulations. The inference about entropy loss (C116) and base-pair melting (C118) is supported by the structural data and MD simulations (C86, C118). These claims integrate multiple lines of evidence into a coherent mechanistic model.

result: MD simulations show that the substrate D'-guide duplex is less stable at the substrate 3' end than the substrate D-guide duplex, and melting of the last two base-pairs results in numerous protein-RNA contacts that stabilize the [on,off]-state. Methylation efficiency is regulated by a complex interaction network depending on the substrate rRNA sequence beyond the methylation site, with different substrate-guide duplexes shifting the equilibrium between [off,off]- and [on,off]-states to modulate methylation levels.
evaluation: Claims C120-C122 are supported by MD simulation data (Figures 6-7). Claim C123 is speculative but reasonable based on the MD results. Claims C124-C125 represent the overall mechanistic conclusion, integrating structural, thermodynamic, and simulation data. The proposed mechanism is well-supported by the evidence, though C125 is somewhat speculative about the in vivo relevance and would benefit from additional experimental validation.

result: When the free-energy difference between active and inactive enzyme states is large and positive, the Box C/D RNP loses its capacity to catalyze methylation, which could be the basis for supporting functions unrelated to methylation.
evaluation: Claims C126-C127 are speculative extrapolations about extreme cases not directly tested in this study. While the logic is sound based on the thermodynamic framework established, there is no experimental evidence for these extreme scenarios. The speculation about orphan snoRNPs (C127) is interesting but unsupported by data in this manuscript. These claims would require additional experimental validation.

result: Background claims establish that 2'-O-rRNA methylation is essential and catalyzed by Box C/D RNPs, with variable methylation levels across species and tissues despite site conservation. The archaeal system serves as a valid proxy for the eukaryotic enzyme based on architectural similarity and comparable methylation complexity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C30, C97-C99, C105 provide background context supported by citations to the literature. These establish the biological importance of rRNA methylation, the role of Box C/D RNPs, and the rationale for using the archaeal system. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature and represent established knowledge in the field. Claim C29 about the validity of the archaeal system as a proxy is a reasonable inference based on structural and functional similarities.
